notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Joshua 10:23–43, drawn from the sources I was able to access:

---

## Joshua 10:23–27 — The Execution of the Five Kings

**v. 23: “So they brought the five kings out of the cave—the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.”**

- Gill notes that the kings are named individually “for the greater glory of the conquest, and the triumph over them” — each name underscores the magnitude of the victory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) observes that Joshua had delayed dealing with the kings so he could finish the battle first; unlike Saul who later sinned by failing to carry out God’s judgment against Agag (1 Samuel 15), Joshua returned to deal with them in due time. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- Guzik also notes a typological observation: Adoni-Zedek (“Lord of Righteousness”) was the pagan king of Jerusalem leading a confederation of kings who fought against Joshua and hid in a cave — a picture of the coming Antichrist (cf. Revelation 6:15–17; 17:12–14). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**v. 24: “Come here and put your feet on the necks of these kings.”**

- This was **not** a barbarous insult but a **symbolic act of complete subjugation**, well attested in ancient Near Eastern practice. JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) calls it “a symbolical action, expressive of a complete victory,” citing Deuteronomy 33:29, Psalm 110:5, and Malachi 4:3. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)
- The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges notes this gesture appears on Assyrian and Egyptian monuments and was practiced even by Byzantine emperors. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary highlights Joshua’s **moral superiority**: he did not place his own foot on the kings’ necks but called the captains (the “cut off” ones, i.e., subordinate officers) to do it — modestly disclaiming personal arrogance while making the point that all Israel would triumph. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)
- Matthew Poole gives four reasons: (1) punishment for impious rebellion against their sovereign Lord, (2) fulfilment of the curse of servility (Genesis 9:25), (3) a token to assure the captains of God’s future subduing of enemies, and (4) to teach Israel not to spare any enemy out of foolish pity or respect for rank — as Saul later spared Agag to his ruin. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)
- Matthew Henry adds that this act fulfilled the promise of Deuteronomy 33:29 (“Thou shalt tread upon their high places”) and served as a type of Christ’s victory: “All the enemies of the Redeemer shall be made his footstool” (Psalm 110:1). He also sees believers’ spiritual victory prefigured: “the God of peace shall tread Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- The Pulpit Commentary preserves a spiritual application from Origen: “Would that my Lord Jesus… grant me to trample underfoot the spirit of fornication, to tread on the necks of the spirit of anger and fury, to trample the demon of greed…” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)

**v. 25: “Do not be afraid or discouraged… Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight.”**

- Constable notes that Joshua strengthened the impact of the symbolic foot-on-neck act “with an encouraging exhortation.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- Guzik sees this as reiterating **partnership with God**: God promised victory “over all your enemies against whom you fight” — those whom Israel actually engaged. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- Matthew Henry explains the twofold purpose: (1) “Fear not these kings” — don’t worry about future revenge for this humiliation; (2) “Fear not any other kings” — since you see these brought low, be confident others will fall too. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)

**v. 26: “Joshua struck down and killed the kings, and he hung their bodies on five trees and left them there until evening.”**

- The hanging was **post-mortem display**, not the method of execution. The bodies were hung for public humiliation and to instill fear in remaining enemies. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- Joshua strictly obeyed Deuteronomy 21:22–23 by taking the bodies down before sundown. Coffman notes that Plummer observed “this law is to be found only in Deuteronomy” — a minute detail supporting Deuteronomy’s authenticity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- Guzik notes that by performing the executions himself, Joshua accepted great risk: “Often rulers will spare other rulers, thinking they might be on the losing side in the future.” Joshua made it clear there could be **absolutely no accommodation** with the Canaanites. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- The hanging on a tree connects to Galatians 3:13 — “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree” — and thus foreshadows Christ becoming a curse for us. (https://biblehub.com/joshua/10-26.htm)

**v. 27: “At sunset Joshua ordered that they be taken down… thrown into the cave… large stones were placed against the mouth.”**

- Constable sees the large stones as “another memorial to God’s faithfulness and power,” parallel to the stones over Achan (Joshua 7:25). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- Guzik highlights the **ironic twist**: “the place they had thought would be their refuge ended up as their tomb.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- Keil & Delitzsch argue that the phrase “unto this very day” (or “until this very day”) does **not** mean a long time elapsed before writing. They translate it as referring to the stones remaining “until that very day” — i.e., the day the kings were fetched out and executed, not the writer’s own time. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)

---

## Joshua 10:28–39 — The Southern Campaign: Seven Cities Conquered

**Overview:** Constable notes that after the battle at Gibeon, seven further victories followed. The writer highlights two things: (1) Israel obeyed God’s command to exterminate the Canaanites in these cities, and (2) it was Yahweh who gave Israel’s enemies into her hands (vv. 30, 32). Constable adds that “archaeology has confirmed that many of these cities did not suffer violent destruction at this time” — the purpose was to destroy military capability and instill fear, not to occupy every site. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)

**v. 28: Makkedah.** Captured “on that day.” The city and its king were devoted to destruction (ḥērem), leaving no survivors — “as he had done to the king of Jericho.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**vv. 29–30: Libnah.** “The LORD also delivered that city and its king into the hand of Israel.” The same pattern: all people put to the sword, no survivors, king treated as Jericho’s king. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**vv. 31–32: Lachish.** Captured “on the second day” — implying resistance strong enough to require a second day of fighting. Still, the LORD delivered it. Guzik: “Each battle was a test. None of them were easy, but under the leadership of Joshua, they all were victorious.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**v. 33: Horam king of Gezer.** He came to help Lachish, but Joshua struck him down along with his people, leaving no survivors. Guzik notes Gezer was an important city guarding a pass; its king’s intervention was futile. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**vv. 34–35: Eglon.** Taken “that day” — a one-day conquest. Same ḥērem pattern as Lachish. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**vv. 36–37: Hebron.** Joshua “went up” from Eglon to Hebron (higher elevation). The destruction extended to “its king, all its villages, and all the people” — “he devoted to destruction Hebron and everyone in it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**vv. 38–39: Debir.** “Finally Joshua… turned toward Debir.” The same comprehensive destruction — king, villages, all people. Guzik: the summary formula “as he had done to Hebron… as he had done to Libnah” shows the consistent, thorough obedience to God’s command. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

---

## Joshua 10:40–43 — Summary of the Southern Conquest

**v. 40: “So Joshua conquered the whole region—the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, and the slopes… leaving no survivors. He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, just as the LORD… had commanded.”**

- Constable is careful: “‘All’ has a limited meaning. In this context it means all parts of the land, all the kings of the cities that Joshua destroyed, and all who lived in those cities (cf. Joshua 13:1).” Israel did **not** defeat every town or kill every Canaanite without exception; rather, Joshua effectively removed the military threat from the south. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- The four geographical regions — hill country, Negev (south), foothills (Shephelah/lowlands), and slopes (wilderness slopes toward the Dead Sea) — give a comprehensive sweep of the southern territory. Guzik calls this “an overview of a region that covers hundreds of square miles.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- The Hebrew term behind “devoted to destruction” is **ḥērem** (charam), meaning irrevocable dedication to God, often by destruction. Precept Austin notes it means “setting something aside strictly for God’s use” — once invoked, it was absolutely compulsory, and the thing devoted could not be redeemed. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-10-commentary)

**v. 41: “Joshua conquered the area from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza, and the whole region of Goshen as far as Gibeon.”**

- Constable clarifies that “Goshen” here is a town in southern Judah (Joshua 15:51), **not** the region of Egypt by that name. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- The geographical sweep runs from the far southern desert (Kadesh-barnea) to the coastal plain (Gaza), and across to Gibeon in the central highlands.

**v. 42: “And because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel, Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign.”**

- This is the theological centre of the entire chapter. Guzik: “This was obviously the most important factor. This illustrates the key aspect in the battle against spiritual enemies for believers. They can only win as they see the Lord fighting on their behalf. He provides the victory, and they walk in it.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- “One campaign” (literally “at one time”) indicates a swift, decisive sweep — a matter of weeks or months, not years.

**v. 43: “Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.”**

- Guzik: “Israel’s victories always came from Gilgal. This was the place of surrendered faith, commitment, and fellowship with God.” Gilgal was the place of memorial (Joshua 4:20), radical obedience (5:2–3), removal of reproach (5:9), and where manna ceased (5:11–12). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)
- Ellicott simply notes Gilgal was “a central position, with Jordan and the conquered territory of the two and a half tribes in the rear.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-10.html)
- Constable quotes Kitchen: “Beyond inflicting immediate loss, this campaign achieved little else by itself — it was a sweep, not an occupation… Occupation of the land, to live in it, keep livestock and cultivate crops in it, etc., was a far slower process.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The sources I could access did not reveal sharp *denominational* disagreements on this particular passage. Most traditions read it similarly. However, subtle differences in emphasis emerge:

**Reformed / Calvinist:** Emphasis falls on **divine sovereignty in judgment**. The Gospel Coalition (Reformed evangelical) stresses that the ḥērem was specific to the theocracy — “Israel was not given a blanket permission to do the same to any peoples they encountered, at any time or in any place.” Christians today are not a theocracy and must not replicate this; the destruction was limited and for clearly stated reasons (Genesis 15:16 — the iniquity of the Amorites was now full). (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/destruction-and-dispossession-of-the-canaanites-in-the-book-of-joshua/)

**Baptist:** The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary underscores simple obedience: “The extinction of the Canaanites was by the orders of the Lord Himself, that the land might be cleansed and its idolatry eradicated.” It draws practical lessons: “bad decisions will soon bring us serious problems… when the victory is sure we are not to rest on our laurels, but continue to make it complete.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-10.html)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic:** David Guzik (Enduring Word, associated with Calvary Chapel / charismatic evangelicalism) emphasises **partnership with God** in victory — “God wants to draw His people into partnership with Him in seeing His work done.” Also, the typological reading of Adoni-Zedek as a picture of Antichrist reflects a futurist / apocalyptic interest characteristic of some charismatic circles. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-10/)

**Lutheran:** Keil & Delitzsch (the standard conservative Lutheran OT commentary of the 19th c.) reads with careful attention to Hebrew grammar and historical context. Keil’s distinctive contribution here is arguing that “until this very day” refers to the day of execution, not a late date of composition — a grammatical defence of early authorship. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)

**Anglican / Methodist:** Matthew Henry (nonconformist but widely used across traditions including Methodist and Anglican) reads the foot-on-neck act through a **typological and devotional** lens — seeing Christ’s victory over Satan and the believer’s spiritual warfare prefigured. The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican, 19th c.) adds the moral reflection that Joshua’s decision to let his captains (not himself) tread on the kings shows “very great moral superiority” over other ancient conquerors. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/10-24.htm)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship / Archaeology:**

- Dr. Thomas Constable (Dispensational / evangelical, but engages scholarship) notes: “Archaeology has confirmed that many of these cities did not suffer violent destruction at this time.” The purpose of Joshua’s raids was to destroy military capability and instil fear — not to raze every settlement permanently. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- Constable also notes the connection to the **Amarna Letters**: around 1400 BC, Canaanite kings wrote frantic appeals to Egypt for help against the “Khapiru” (possibly the Hebrews). Egypt under Amenhotep II and his successors had lost interest in Canaanite affairs, leaving the city-states vulnerable — a providential political opening for Israel’s conquest. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/10-23.html)
- The Gospel Coalition article by a conservative scholar argues that the biblical text emphasises **dispossession more than annihilation**: “A careful reading of the biblical texts reveals that God’s commands were more focused on driving the Canaanites out of the land than they were on killing every last, living person… there was no genocide in the sense commonly understood.” The ḥērem language is in part rhetorical, describing total dedication rather than literal extermination of every individual. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/destruction-and-dispossession-of-the-canaanites-in-the-book-of-joshua/)

**Catholic and Orthodox Readings:**

I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on these verses from the approved sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) within the search and fetch limits. The Catholic tradition generally reads Joshua typologically — Joshua (Yeshua/Jesus) as a type of Christ leading God’s people into the promised land, with the Canaanite kings representing the powers of sin and darkness to be conquered. This is consistent with Origen’s spiritual reading preserved in the Pulpit Commentary (see v. 24 above). A fuller Catholic treatment would likely be found in the Haydock Bible Commentary or the Navarre Bible, but those were not reached.

**Debated Popular Modern Teaching:**

No material emerged from the searches specifically addressing prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of this passage. These traditions tend to treat Joshua’s conquest as a model for “possessing your possessions” and claiming victory over life’s obstacles. The tone of Guzik’s application — “God provides the victory, and they walk in it” — is consistent with a broadly charismatic emphasis on claiming God’s promises, though Guzik does not veer into prosperity teaching.

---

These would be valuable for rounding out the “other views” section, particularly the Catholic typological reading and modern critical perspectives on the historicity of the conquest narrative.
